**(CNN)** — After nearly 150 years in business, the *Rocky Mountain News* published its final edition Friday, falling victim to a faltering economy and the rise of the Internet generation. Based in Denver, Colorado, the paper brought its 150-year legacy to a close with that last edition.

Its final front-page headline read, with striking simplicity: "Goodbye, Colorado."

"It is with great sadness that we say goodbye to you today. Our time chronicling the life of Denver and Colorado, the nation and the world, is over."

The newspaper's owner, E.W. Scripps Co., delivered the announcement to the newsroom at noon Thursday, bringing to an end three months of speculation and turmoil surrounding the paper's future. The *News* had been placed on the market in December.

The *Rocky Mountain News* stands as the latest casualty in an era of closures, layoffs and cutbacks that has beset the newspaper industry. "It's in a free fall, and nobody knows where the bottom is. It's kind of like water in the toilet swirling around, and nobody knows what's left when you're done flushing," observed media critic Eric Alterman. *Watch how the economy and Internet are taking a toll on the industry »*

Newspapers across the nation are under mounting pressure as both readership and advertising revenue decline, while a growing number of Americans turn to the Internet for their information. "All newspapers are under great pressure. They'll survive, but they'll survive in different forms; their cost base will have to be dramatically lowered," said Mort Zuckerman, publisher of the *New York Daily News*, which ranks seventh in circulation nationwide.

The steep drop in advertising revenue amid a punishing economy has compelled newspapers to reduce costs by dismissing cartoonists, columnists and others, leaving them to seek employment in an already struggling industry. Pia Catton lost her position as arts editor of the *New York Sun* five months ago, when the paper folded. Though she has taken on a short-term assignment editing a book, she suspects she may soon need to consider a change of career. "There will always be a market for news; you will always need to know immediately what's happening. Will there be a market for newspapers? That's another question," she remarked.

The *Rocky Mountain News* employed more than 200 editorial staff members, according to the Columbia Journalism Review's website.

Rich Boehne, chief executive officer of Scripps, told employees that the newspaper had fallen victim to a dire economy, an upheaval within the newspaper industry and multimillion-dollar annual losses. "Denver can't support two newspapers any longer," Boehne said. "It's certainly not good news for you, and it's certainly not good news for Denver."

Since 2001, the *News* had operated under a joint operating agreement with *The Denver Post*, which merged the two papers' business operations to cut costs while keeping their editorial departments separate. The closure of the *News* leaves Denver, like most American cities, with a single major newspaper.

"We've been, sort of, hanging on the edge for so long," said Mel Pompanio, a presentation editor for the paper. "What a huge loss for Colorado today."

This week, the *San Francisco Chronicle* announced that it faced the prospect of being sold or shut down unless it could halt its losses, which run into the millions. Officials from the Hearst Corp., owners of the *Chronicle*, said the paper lost $50 million in 2008 and is on pace to lose even more this year.

"It's difficult. It's hard," said Lynn Bartels, a political reporter and 26-year employee of Scripps, reflecting on the closure of the *News*. "I haven't returned any phone calls yet, because I don't need to be reporting and crying at the same time. I've done that enough."

Somber expressions filled the newsroom in video posted on the paper's website. A few muffled sobs could also be heard as the reality of the closure began to settle in among the employees.

"I could say stupid things like 'I know how you feel.' I don't," Boehne said. "We are just deeply sorry. I hope you will accept that."

*CNN's Richard Roth contributed to this report.*

After nearly 150 years of continuous publication, the *Rocky Mountain News* rolled off the presses for the final time, marking the end of one of Denver's most storied journalistic institutions. The decision to shut down the venerable newspaper came from its owner, the E.W. Scripps Company, which could no longer justify keeping the operation running amid mounting financial losses. For a paper that had chronicled the city's history since before Colorado achieved statehood, the closure represented far more than the loss of a single publication—it stood as a stark symbol of the profound crisis engulfing the entire newspaper industry.

Print readership had been steadily eroding for years as audiences increasingly turned to the internet for their daily news. With free content available at the click of a mouse, fewer people saw the need to pay for a physical newspaper delivered to their doorstep. Compounding this problem was a dramatic decline in advertising revenue, historically the lifeblood of the newspaper business. Advertisers who once relied on print classifieds and display ads migrated to online platforms, draining papers of the income they needed to sustain their newsrooms and operations.

The demise of the Denver institution was not an isolated event but rather part of a sweeping, industry-wide collapse. Across the nation, newspapers responded to shrinking revenues with waves of layoffs, painful budget cutbacks, and, in the most severe cases, complete shutdowns. Once-thriving publications found themselves slashing staff, reducing coverage, and scaling back the ambitious journalism that had defined their missions. The pattern repeated itself in city after city, leaving communities with fewer voices to report on local government, business, culture, and civic life.

For the journalists who dedicated their careers to these publications, the consequences were deeply personal. Professionals like Pia Catton, the former arts editor, found themselves displaced and compelled to seek employment elsewhere, often in fields far removed from the newsrooms where they had built their expertise. Their experiences reflected the human toll of an industry in freefall—talented reporters, editors, and photographers whose livelihoods evaporated as the traditional business model crumbled beneath them.

Ultimately, the closure of the *Rocky Mountain News* served as a powerful warning to the newspaper world. It made clear that survival in the digital age would require more than incremental adjustments or hopeful waiting for conditions to improve. To endure, newspapers would need to fundamentally reinvent how they operated—rethinking their revenue streams, embracing digital innovation, and finding new ways to deliver value to readers and advertisers alike. The old formula was no longer sustainable, and the papers that failed to transform themselves risked following the *Rocky Mountain News* into history.

# Rocky Mountain News Publishes Final Edition After Nearly 150 Years

**Denver's oldest newspaper falls victim to economic downturn and shifting media landscape**

DENVER — The Rocky Mountain News, one of Colorado's most storied newspapers, published its final edition Friday, ending a nearly 150-year run that spanned the state's transformation from frontier territory to modern hub of the American West.

The closure comes just weeks shy of the paper's 150th anniversary, a milestone the newsroom had hoped to celebrate but will now never reach. The final edition featured a somber front page and extensive coverage of the newspaper's long history and its role in chronicling the region's most significant moments.

"It is with great sadness that we say goodbye to you today," the newspaper told its readers in an emotional farewell that acknowledged the profound loss felt by staff and the community alike.

## A Casualty of Industry-Wide Struggles

The Rocky Mountain News joins a growing list of American newspapers grappling with the twin pressures of a devastating economic recession and the fundamental disruption caused by the internet. As readers increasingly turn to online sources for their news and advertisers follow the audience to digital platforms, traditional print revenues have plummeted.

The newspaper's parent company, E.W. Scripps Co., had put the publication up for sale, but was unable to find a buyer willing to take on the struggling operation amid one of the worst advertising climates in decades.

The decline in classified advertising—once a reliable financial backbone for print newspapers—has been particularly damaging as online competitors offer free or low-cost alternatives.

## Award-Winning Journalism

Throughout its history, the Rocky Mountain News earned a reputation for excellence, winning multiple Pulitzer Prizes for its coverage. The paper distinguished itself with powerful photojournalism and in-depth reporting on stories of both local and national significance.

Founded in 1859 during the Colorado gold rush era, the News witnessed and documented the birth and growth of Denver and the surrounding region. For generations of Coloradans, the newspaper was an integral part of daily life.

## Staff and Community React

The closure leaves scores of journalists and other employees without jobs at a time when opportunities in the newspaper industry are increasingly scarce. Newsroom veterans expressed shock and grief as the reality of the shutdown set in.

The loss of the Rocky Mountain News reduces the diversity of voices in Denver's media market and raises concerns among industry observers about the future of local journalism in communities across the nation.

## A Troubling Trend

The demise of the Rocky Mountain News is being watched closely as a bellwether for the newspaper industry as a whole. Publications in cities across the country are facing similar financial pressures, with some cutting staff, reducing publication days, or shutting down entirely.

Media analysts warn that the loss of established newspapers could leave gaps in coverage of local government, schools, and community institutions that other media outlets may struggle to fill.

As the presses fall silent, the closure of the Rocky Mountain News marks the end of an era—not just for Denver, but as a stark symbol of the challenges confronting American journalism in the digital age.

# The Cleveland Standard Ceases Publication After 147 Years, Marking Latest Casualty in Newspaper Industry's Decline

*By Staff Report*

CLEVELAND — The Cleveland Standard, one of Ohio's oldest and most respected daily newspapers, will print its final edition this Sunday, ending nearly a century and a half of continuous publication and leaving more than 200 employees without jobs.

The announcement, made Tuesday morning by parent company Meridian Media Group, cited "insurmountable financial headwinds" and a collapse in print advertising revenue as the primary drivers behind the decision to shutter the publication founded in 1877.

## A Difficult Decision

"This is one of the most painful decisions I have made in my forty years in this industry," said Margaret Ellison, CEO of Meridian Media Group, during a somber press conference at the paper's downtown headquarters. "The Standard has served this community with distinction through world wars, economic depressions, and profound social change. But the economic reality is that we can no longer sustain operations."

Ellison noted that the paper's print advertising revenue had declined more than 70 percent over the past decade, while digital subscriptions failed to offset the losses.

"We tried everything—paywalls, membership models, events, partnerships," she said. "The math simply stopped working."

## Newsroom Reaction

For the journalists inside the newsroom, the announcement landed with a mixture of grief and resignation.

"I've given twenty-three years to this paper," said Robert Chen, a veteran investigative reporter whose work exposed corruption in the county water department. "We broke stories that changed people's lives. To watch it end like this feels like losing a member of the family."

Younger staff members expressed anxiety about the future of the profession itself.

"I graduated from journalism school five years ago believing there was still a path forward," said Ashley Morrison, a city hall reporter. "Now I'm not sure what comes next—for me or for the communities that depend on local coverage. Who's going to sit through those seven-hour zoning meetings now?"

The paper's longtime editor-in-chief, David Kaminski, struck a defiant but mournful tone in an emotional address to the newsroom.

"We did the work. We held power accountable. We told the truth, even when it was inconvenient," Kaminski told his staff, according to attendees. "Never let anyone tell you this work didn't matter. It mattered more than ever."

## Industry Experts Weigh In

Media analysts described the closure as emblematic of a broader crisis facing local journalism across the United States.

"The Cleveland Standard is not an outlier—it's a symptom," said Dr. Patricia Nwosu, a professor of media economics at Northwestern University. "We've lost more than a third of the nation's newspapers since 2005. What we're witnessing is the systematic hollowing out of local accountability journalism."

Nwosu pointed to the rise of "news deserts"—communities without any dedicated local news coverage—as a growing threat to civic engagement.

"When a paper like this dies, corruption goes unreported, voter participation drops, and communities become more polarized," she said. "The consequences extend far beyond the people who lose their jobs."

Tom Bradley, a media critic and former newspaper editor, offered a blunter assessment.

"The tech platforms swallowed the advertising revenue that sustained journalism for a century and gave nothing back," Bradley said. "We built an information ecosystem that rewards outrage over reporting. The Standard's closure should be a wake-up call, but I fear we've hit the snooze button too many times already."

## A Community Responds

Reaction from Cleveland residents and civic leaders was swift.

"The Standard was the conscience of this city," said Mayor Angela Reyes in a statement. "Its reporters asked the hard questions that politicians like me didn't always want to answer. Democracy is weaker today."

Longtime subscriber Harold Fitzgerald, 78, expressed his dismay outside the paper's headquarters, holding a worn copy of that morning's edition.

"I've read this paper every morning with my coffee since I was a young man," Fitzgerald said. "It doesn't feel real that tomorrow it just won't be there."

## What Comes Next

Meridian Media Group indicated that the Standard's digital archives would be preserved and that a small team might be retained to maintain a limited online presence, though details remained unclear.

Industry observers note that some communities have experimented with nonprofit journalism models and reader-funded newsrooms as alternatives to the failing commercial model.

"There is hope in these new experiments," Dr. Nwosu said. "But they cannot yet replace the scale and institutional memory of a legacy newsroom. When you lose 147 years of accumulated knowledge, you cannot simply rebuild it overnight."

The Cleveland Standard's final edition will be distributed Sunday, featuring a retrospective on the paper's history and a farewell message from its staff.

"We were here," Kaminski said. "We mattered. And I hope someone, somewhere, picks up where we left off."

---

# Denver's Oldest Newspaper Silenced After Nearly 150 Years

**DENVER, Colorado** — The presses of the Rocky Mountain News fell silent Friday, ending a nearly 150-year run and marking one of the most significant casualties yet in the newspaper industry's deepening crisis.

The Denver institution, founded in 1859 just weeks before Colorado's gold rush transformed the region, published its final edition Friday, leaving hundreds of employees without jobs and a community without one of its defining voices.

"This is like losing a member of the family," said longtime subscriber Margaret Ellison, 72, clutching a copy of the final edition outside the paper's downtown offices. "I've read the Rocky every morning for over 50 years. I don't know what tomorrow will look like."

## A Sudden End

Parent company E.W. Scripps announced the closure after failing to find a buyer for the paper, which had been on the market for weeks. Executives cited catastrophic advertising declines and the accelerating shift of readers to online platforms.

"This is a decision that breaks our hearts," a Scripps spokesperson said. "The Rocky Mountain News has been an extraordinary institution, but the economic realities facing our industry made continued operation impossible."

The newspaper, which won four Pulitzer Prizes in the past decade, employed roughly 200 staff members in its newsroom.

## Newsroom in Mourning

Inside the building, veteran journalists described a scene of disbelief and grief as they assembled their last edition.

"We put out a great paper right up until the very end," said one reporter, his voice cracking. "That's what makes this so painful. We were doing award-winning work, and it still wasn't enough to survive."

Reporters spoke of clearing out desks that held decades of memories, of covering their own newspaper's death as a final assignment.

"I've reported on layoffs, on companies closing, on communities losing their livelihoods," said a business editor who asked not to be named. "I never imagined I'd be writing that story about my own newsroom."

## Industry Experts Warn of Larger Crisis

Media analysts said the shutdown reflects an existential threat facing American newspapers as the recession compounds long-term structural challenges.

"The Rocky Mountain News is not an isolated case—it's a warning," said a media economics professor at a leading journalism school. "We're watching a fundamental pillar of local democracy erode in real time. When a paper like this dies, communities lose their watchdog."

Industry observers pointed to plummeting print advertising revenue, mounting debt loads at parent companies, and the failure of digital revenue to offset losses.

"The economics simply stopped working," said a newspaper industry consultant. "For years, papers subsidized robust newsrooms with classified and display advertising. That model has collapsed, and nothing has replaced it at scale."

## Questions About Local Coverage

The closure leaves Denver a one-newspaper town and raises concerns about the future of accountability journalism in the region.

"Who covers the city council now? Who investigates local corruption? Who tells the stories that don't make national headlines?" asked a former editor. "These are the questions that should worry every citizen, not just journalists."

## A Legacy Remembered

Founded 55 days before Colorado officially became a territory, the Rocky Mountain News chronicled the state's evolution from frontier settlement to modern metropolis, covering everything from gold rushes to Super Bowls.

For the journalists gathering their belongings Friday, the loss transcended employment.

"This was more than a job," said a photographer who spent two decades at the paper. "It was a calling. And now it's gone."

As staff members left the building for the final time, some paused to take photographs of the sign bearing the newspaper's name—documenting, one last time, the end of an era.

The American newspaper industry, battered by a collapsing advertising market and the relentless migration of readers to the internet, suffered a series of devastating blows in early 2009 as historic publications shuttered their doors or teetered on the brink of collapse.

## The Rocky Mountain News Goes Dark

Colorado's oldest newspaper, the Rocky Mountain News, published its final edition on February 27, 2009, just weeks shy of its 150th anniversary. The closure brought to an end nearly a century and a half of continuous publication that had begun in 1859, during the days of the Colorado Gold Rush.

The paper's owner, E.W. Scripps Company, announced the shutdown after failing to find a buyer for the struggling publication. The News had been losing money at an unsustainable rate, and the broader economic downturn made a rescue increasingly unlikely.

The Rocky, as it was affectionately known to Denver readers, was no ordinary newspaper. It had earned four Pulitzer Prizes in the years before its closure, distinguishing itself with award-winning photography and investigative journalism. Its demise left hundreds of employees out of work and marked one of the most significant losses in what was shaping up to be a catastrophic year for print media.

The closure was particularly poignant given how close the paper came to its sesquicentennial milestone—a testament to the industry's rapid decline that a publication surviving 149 years could not endure its final months.

## The Chronicle's Uncertain Future

In San Francisco, the venerable Chronicle faced its own existential crisis. Its parent company, Hearst Corporation, issued a stark warning in early 2009 that the paper could be sold or shut down entirely if significant cost reductions could not be achieved quickly.

The Chronicle had been hemorrhaging money, reportedly losing tens of millions of dollars annually. Hearst demanded major concessions and staff reductions as it sought to stem the losses. The prospect of a major American city like San Francisco losing its primary daily newspaper underscored the severity of the crisis gripping the industry.

## The New York Sun's Setting

## An Industry in Crisis

These high-profile casualties were symptoms of a broader collapse. Newspapers across the country faced plummeting advertising revenue as businesses cut spending during the recession and classified advertising—long a financial cornerstone—migrated to free online platforms.

Major newspaper companies filed for bankruptcy protection during this period, and publications everywhere slashed staff, reduced page counts, and cut publication days in desperate attempts to survive. The combination of cyclical economic pressures and the structural transformation of how people consumed news created what many observers called a perfect storm.

## A Turning Point for Journalism

The events of 2009 raised profound questions about the future of local journalism and the civic role newspapers had traditionally played. As cities faced the possibility of becoming "news deserts," concerns mounted about who would hold local governments accountable and cover community affairs in the absence of established newsrooms.

For the readers of the Rocky Mountain News and the countless journalists who lost their livelihoods, 2009 represented not just an economic downturn but the end of an era—a stark reminder that even institutions with deep historical roots were not immune to the sweeping changes reshaping American media.

# The Final Edition: How Economic Collapse and Digital Disruption Killed a Newspaper Institution

On February 27, 2009, the *Rocky Mountain News* published its last edition, its front page bearing a simple, heartbreaking headline: "Goodbye, Colorado." After nearly 150 years of chronicling the life of a state—from frontier settlement through statehood, war, boom, and bust—the newspaper folded just weeks shy of its 150th anniversary. Its death has since become one of the most emblematic stories of an industry in freefall.

## A Storied History Cut Short

Founded in 1859 by William Byers, the *Rocky Mountain News* predated Colorado's statehood by 17 years. For generations, it served as an essential thread in the civic fabric of Denver and the surrounding region, winning four Pulitzer Prizes in the decade before its closure—including recognition for its coverage of the Columbine High School shooting. By any measure of journalistic quality, the paper was thriving. By the measure that increasingly mattered—revenue—it was dying.

The final edition ran 52 pages and included a documentary-style farewell, complete with a moving video that captured the newsroom's final hours. Staff members wept openly. The message to readers was clear: this was not a failure of talent or dedication, but of a business model that could no longer support the work.

## The Perfect Storm

The demise of the *Rocky Mountain News* resulted from the collision of two powerful and reinforcing forces: a catastrophic economic downturn and the structural upheaval brought by online media.

### The Recession's Toll

When the E.W. Scripps Company put the *Rocky* up for sale in December 2008, the nation was mired in the Great Recession. Advertising—the lifeblood of any newspaper—was collapsing. Businesses slashed their marketing budgets, and the classified advertising that once filled pages with job listings, car sales, and real estate notices evaporated almost overnight.

Scripps reported that the newspaper had lost $16 million in 2008 alone. With the economy in tatters, no buyer emerged for a property hemorrhaging money in a shrinking market. The recession didn't merely wound the *Rocky*; it removed any hope of rescue.

### The Digital Disruption

Yet the recession only accelerated a decline that was already well underway. The deeper, more permanent threat came from the internet, which fundamentally dismantled the economics that had sustained newspapers for more than a century.

Classified advertising, once a reliable profit engine, migrated to free or low-cost online platforms like Craigslist. Display advertisers found cheaper, more targeted options on the web. Meanwhile, readers grew accustomed to consuming news online for free, unwilling to pay for content when endless alternatives sat a click away.

Newspapers found themselves caught in an impossible bind. They needed to maintain expensive newsrooms—reporters, editors, photographers, printing presses, and delivery fleets—while their traditional revenue streams dried up and their digital offerings generated only a fraction of the income lost. The *Rocky Mountain News* competed in a two-newspaper town alongside *The Denver Post*, making the market especially vulnerable when advertising dollars grew scarce.

## A Symbol of a Broader Crisis

The closure of the *Rocky* was not an isolated tragedy. It was a bellwether. Within the same period, the *Seattle Post-Intelligencer* ceased print publication, the Tribune Company filed for bankruptcy, and hundreds of newspapers across the country cut staff, reduced circulation, or shut down entirely.

The consequences extend far beyond the industry itself. Newspapers have long performed a vital democratic function—holding local governments accountable, covering city councils and school boards, and investigating corruption that would otherwise go unexposed. When a paper like the *Rocky* dies, it creates a "news desert," leaving communities with fewer watchdogs and less information about the institutions that shape their lives.

## The Lingering Question

More than a decade later, the questions raised by the *Rocky Mountain News*'s final edition remain unresolved. The industry has experimented with paywalls, nonprofit models, philanthropic funding, and digital subscriptions, with mixed success. Some outlets have found sustainable footing; many others continue to struggle or disappear.

The "Goodbye, Colorado" edition endures as a poignant monument to what was lost—and as a warning. It reminds us that the collapse of the newspaper industry is not simply a business story about failing companies. It is a story about the erosion of an institution that helped communities understand themselves and hold power to account. The economic and technological forces that killed the *Rocky* have not relented, and the search for a viable path forward for local journalism continues to this day.
